h1: The 8 Best Toaster Ovens for RVs of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Toaster Ovens for RVs: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 toaster ovens for RV galleys compared on size, wattage draw and safety features, from Elite Gourmet to Breville.
summary: The Elite Gourmet ETO449X is the best toaster oven for RVs: marketed for RV use, an 800W draw, a compact 8.99L cavity and a cool-touch handle, for $25 to $50. The ETO490 adds a 30 minute timer, the ETO236 is the most compact, and the Dash Mini is the cheap backup with auto shutoff. The Breville BOV650XL is a hard fit for most rigs.
intro: An RV galley has two hard limits a house kitchen does not: counter space measured in inches and a power budget that a shared 30 amp hookup or a generator can run dry in a hurry. A toaster oven that looks tiny in a photo can still trip a breaker alongside the air conditioner, or refuse to fit the cabinet where it must live while the rig is moving.

We reviewed eight toaster ovens, from compact two-slice units to larger smart ovens. Each was ranked on how it uses space, the wattage it draws where the listing states one, and the safety details that matter when the kitchen moves. Where a listing gives no wattage, we say so, because an unknown draw is a planning risk on a small generator.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ETO449X Toaster Oven
products.verdict: Marketed for RVs, 800W, compact 8.99L and a cool-touch handle. The sensible default.
products.description:
The ETO449X is explicitly marketed for RV use, with a stated 800W draw, a compact 8.99L cavity and a cool-touch handle. It fits four slices and has a pizza function, and sells for $25 to $50. A stated wattage is the most useful number in this guide, because it lets you add the oven to your generator budget before you buy.

It beats the ETO490 on one number: 800W is gentler on a small generator, and the cavity is almost the same size. Compared with the Breville, it is far smaller but also far lighter on power, at less than half the wattage. The trade is basic controls and no convection.

Buy it if you boondock or share a 30 amp circuit and want an oven that suits the setup. The caveat is the small cavity. Skip it if you cook for a crowd or want convection.
products.idealFor: RVers who need low wattage and a small footprint.
products.skipIf: You want convection or a big cavity.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ETO490 9L/4-Slice Oven
products.verdict: A 9L, 4-slice oven with a thermostat and 30 minute timer. Real baking in a tiny space.
products.description:
The ETO490 holds four slices in a 9L cavity, with a built-in thermostat to keep temperature steady and a 30 minute timer. It sells for $25 to $50. A thermostat matters in a tiny oven because small cavities swing in temperature fast, and a timer that long is enough for roasting and baking, not just toast.

It sits one rung behind the ETO449X because that model lists its 800W draw and RV marketing outright, while the ETO490 leaves wattage out of the summary. Against the 2-slice ETO236, it adds a longer timer and more room for a small pan.

A strong choice for RV cooks who want more than toast. The caveat is that wattage is unlisted, so check it on the listing before plugging into a small inverter. Skip it if your power budget is tight and unconfirmed.
products.idealFor: RV cooks who want to bake as well as toast.
products.skipIf: Your power budget is tight and unconfirmed.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ETO236 Compact 2-Slice Toaster Oven
products.verdict: The smallest oven here, with a short 15 minute timer. Ideal for tiny galleys.
products.description:
The ETO236 is a compact 2-slice toaster oven with a built-in thermostat and a short 15 minute timer. It sells for $25 to $50. A short timer limits cooking time, which in practice caps how long the heating element draws power, a small plus on a thin power budget. It is the one that disappears into a cabinet most easily.

It trails the two bigger Elite Gourmet models because a 15 minute timer limits what you can cook, and two slices suit one or two people only. Compared with the Dash, it has a proper thermostat and a bit more room.

Pick it if counter space is the main constraint and you mostly reheat and toast. The caveat is that it cannot roast a meal. Skip it if you cook full meals in the RV.
products.idealFor: Couples and solo travelers with very little counter.
products.skipIf: You cook full meals in the RV.

products.name: Dash Mini Toaster Oven
products.verdict: Light, cheap and it shuts itself off. A reasonable small-space backup.
products.description:
The Dash Mini is a compact, light oven with a pizza function and an auto shutoff, which is a genuine safety plus in a moving vehicle. It is the least expensive pick in the roundup, under $25. An auto shutoff cuts the heat if you forget it, which matters when a road trip distracts you.

It ranks below the Elite Gourmet trio because their listings are more specific about thermostat and timer features. Against the ETO236, it trades a thermostat for the shutoff and a lower price. Light weight makes it easy to stow in a locker when the rig moves.

A nice choice for a weekend camper who wants a cheap secondary cooker. The caveat is a small cavity and few temperature details. Skip it if you cook in your RV every day.
products.idealFor: Weekend campers who want a cheap backup oven.
products.skipIf: You cook in your RV every day.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 4-Slice Toaster Oven with Natural Convection
products.verdict: Four cooking modes and natural convection for a middle-of-the-road price.
products.description:
This BLACK+DECKER offers four cooking modes covering bake, broil, toast and warm, with natural convection to even out heat. It fits four slices and sells for $50 to $100. Four modes let one box replace a small oven for broiling cheese or warming rolls, which a basic toaster oven handles poorly.

It ranks below the Elite Gourmet trio for RV use because its listing does not state a wattage, which makes power planning a guess. Compared with the TO1313SBD, it is the better-rounded option. Against the ETO490, it costs a bracket more and runs bulkier.

Best for RVers with a bigger rig who want more cooking range. The caveat is the unlisted wattage, so confirm the draw before relying on a generator. Skip it if you run on a small inverter.
cons: Bulkier than the Elite Gourmet picks
products.idealFor: Larger rigs where cooking variety matters.
products.skipIf: You run on a small inverter.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER TO1313SBD Toaster Oven
products.verdict: A curved interior that fits a 9-inch pizza or four slices. Roomy for the class.
products.description:
The TO1313SBD has a curved interior that fits a 9-inch pizza or four slices, which is more capacity than a basic 2-slice model. It also lists convection and sells for $50 to $100. A curved cavity gives a round pizza room without wasting corners, a plus in a space-limited galley.

It lands below the other BLACK+DECKER because it is the older, plainer design, and it gives up the specific four-mode controls. It is larger than the Elite Gourmet picks, so cabinet fit is the question. Like the other BLACK+DECKER, it lists no wattage.

A good fit for a larger RV kitchen cooking for two or three people. The caveat is the bigger footprint and unlisted wattage. Measure your counter before ordering, and skip it if counter space is very limited.
products.idealFor: RV kitchens feeding two or three people.

products.name: Breville BOV450XL Mini Smart Oven
products.verdict: The smallest Breville with its five-quartz-element system. Premium, but costly.
products.description:
The BOV450XL is the smallest Breville in the lineup and uses the same five-quartz-element Element iQ system as larger models. Its stainless steel body is a step above the plastic competition. It sells for $100 to $200. Quartz elements respond fast, so they heat the part of the cavity that needs it.

It ranks lower for RV use because the price is several times the Elite Gourmet picks and the listing gives no wattage. It does beat the BOV650XL on counter space, since it is smaller. Against the ETO449X, it is a premium result in a similar footprint.

Buy it if you live in the RV and want premium results. The caveat is cost and unknown draw. Check your power source first, and skip it if you cook occasionally or run on a small generator.
pros: Better fit for RV counters than larger Brevilles
products.idealFor: Full-timers who want premium results in a small body.
products.skipIf: You cook occasionally or run on a small generator.

products.name: Breville BOV650XL Compact Smart Oven
products.verdict: Fits a 12-inch pizza and preheats fast on 1800W. Great oven, hard on an RV.
products.description:
The BOV650XL fits a 12-inch pizza or a small roast, and its 1800W element preheats quickly. It uses the same Element iQ system as other Brevilles and sells for $100 to $200. Nearly two kilowatts of draw is enormous for a rig, since 1800W is more than twice the ETO449X's 800W.

It finishes last because 1800W is a heavy draw for many RV hookups and generators, and the footprint is the largest here. Against the BOV450XL, it gives you more room at the cost of power and space.

Only buy it for a large rig on a strong shore power connection. The caveat is the draw that can trip a 30 amp circuit beside the air conditioner. Everyone else will fit better with an Elite Gourmet. Skip it if you boondock.
products.idealFor: Big rigs on stable shore power.
products.skipIf: You boondock or share a small generator.

whatMatters.detail: A toaster oven can draw anything from 800W to 1800W. A shared 30 amp circuit or a small inverter may not carry the bigger ones along with the air conditioner. Look for the wattage on the listing, and compare it with your generator or inverter rating before you buy. The ETO449X lists 800W and the BOV650XL 1800W.

whatMatters.factor: Measure the cabinet, not just the counter
whatMatters.detail: Many RV ovens live in a cabinet between uses. Measure width, depth and height, and leave a few inches behind and above for heat to escape. A unit that fits the counter in a photo may be too tall for the cabinet you plan to use. The ETO236 and Dash Mini are the easiest to stow.

In a moving RV, a hot door or handle is more dangerous than at home. Check for a cool-touch handle, as on the ETO449X, or an auto shutoff, as on the Dash Mini, and secure the oven whenever you drive, regardless of what the listing promises. Unplug it before travel, and never run it while driving.

A 15 minute timer is fine for toast and reheating but too short for roasting. Look for 30 minutes or more if you plan to bake, as on the ETO490, and confirm the timer range in the product bullets rather than relying on a general description. The ETO236's 15 minutes limits it to light work, so bakers should look higher up the list.

Convection moves air around the food so it cooks more evenly and often faster. It matters for baking and roasting, but basic toasting and reheating do not need it. Look for the word convection in the listing, as on the BLACK+DECKER models, and note that it may raise the price and the footprint.

faq.q: How much power does a toaster oven use in an RV?
faq.a: It varies. The Elite Gourmet ETO449X lists 800W while the Breville BOV650XL lists 1800W. Check the wattage against your generator or inverter before buying, and remember other appliances share the circuit. A kettle and an air conditioner running together add up quickly.

faq.q: Can I run a toaster oven on an inverter?
faq.a: Only if the inverter can handle the wattage. A small unit like the ETO449X is a safer bet than a Breville BOV650XL. Always check the continuous rating, not the peak, since an overloaded inverter shuts down mid-bake.

faq.q: Is a convection toaster oven worth it in an RV?
faq.a: For baking and roasting, yes. For toast and reheating, no. Convection models like the BLACK+DECKER 4-Slice are bulkier, which can matter in a tiny galley. A basic oven like the ETO449X is lighter and draws less power.

faq.q: Do I need to secure a toaster oven when driving?
faq.a: Yes. Unplug it, let it cool and stow it in a cabinet or strap it down. A cool-touch handle helps, but it does not make it safe to leave loose. Remove the crumb tray and tape the door shut.

faq.q: Is the Elite Gourmet ETO490 better than the ETO449X?
faq.a: The ETO490 has a 30 minute timer and a 9L cavity. The ETO449X lists 800W and RV marketing. Pick based on whether power or cooking time matters more, and check the ETO490 wattage on the live listing.

faq.q: Can a toaster oven replace a microwave in an RV?
faq.a: For many meals, yes. It bakes, toasts and reheats, though it is slower for liquids. The ETO490 and Breville models are the most flexible here. Plan on a longer wait for boiling water than a microwave gives.

finalTake: Buy the Elite Gourmet ETO449X for most rigs, since its stated 800W draw and compact size suit a shared 30 amp circuit. Choose the ETO490 for more baking time, the ETO236 for a tiny galley and the Dash Mini as a backup. Skip the Breville BOV650XL unless you have strong shore power. Check wattage and cabinet size first.
